plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.6.1
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the unit circle with a fixed angle c and a variable angle x measured from the positive horizontal axis, illustrating the continuity of the sine and cosine functions. Point Q(cos c, sin c) is marked in blue at angle c, and point P(cos x, sin x) is marked in red at angle x; an arrow indicates that P moves toward Q as x approaches c. A caption box at the bottom reads: As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q. The figure provides a geometric motivation for the limits lim_{x->c} sin x = sin c and lim_{x->c} cos x = cos c, establishing that sin and cos are continuous at every point c.

interactionPlan.concept: As the angle x approaches a fixed angle c, the point P(cos x, sin x) slides along the unit circle to the point Q(cos c, sin c), giving the geometric reason that lim(x→c) sin x = sin c and lim(x→c) cos x = cos c — sine and cosine are continuous everywhere.
elements: horizontal axis with arrowhead (positive direction to the right)
vertical axis with arrowhead (positive direction upward)
unit circle centered at the origin, drawn in blue; the right portion solid, the upper-left and lower-left arcs dashed
fixed point Q at angle c, drawn as a blue dot, labeled 'Q(cos c, sin c)'
variable point P at angle x, drawn as a red dot, labeled 'P(cos x, sin x)'
black radius from the origin to Q
red radius from the origin to P
angle arc from the positive horizontal axis to the radius OQ, labeled 'c'
angle arc from the positive horizontal axis to the radius OP, labeled 'x'
shaded sector between the radii at angles x and c, filled with a purple radial gradient
curved arrow near Q, tangent to the circle, indicating the direction P travels as x → c
live numeric readout showing x, c, and the coordinates (cos x, sin x) vs (cos c, sin c)
caption box below the figure with a light gray border: 'As x approaches c the point P approaches the point Q.'

interactions.label: Angle x (radians)
interactions.teaches: Dragging x toward c slides P along the circle toward Q while the shaded sector shrinks to nothing — the learner sees that closing the angle gap forces (cos x, sin x) to land exactly on (cos c, sin c), which is precisely the statement that the limits equal the function values

interactions.label: Target angle c (radians)
interactions.teaches: Relocating Q to any position on the circle — any quadrant, any angle — shows the same convergence behavior, so the learner understands continuity holds at every point c, not just the one drawn in the textbook

interactions.label: Animate x → c from both sides
interactions.teaches: Watching x sweep up to c from below and then down to c from above shows P converging on Q from both directions along the circle, making concrete that the limit is two-sided — left and right approaches land on the same point Q

demo_steps.title: The setup
demo_steps.narration: Q sits at the fixed angle c; P sits at the variable angle x. The shaded sector is the angular gap between them, and P's coordinates (cos x, sin x) differ from Q's (cos c, sin c) by exactly that gap.

demo_steps.title: Close the gap
demo_steps.narration: Drag the x slider toward c: P slides along the circle, the purple sector pinches down to zero area, and P's coordinates in the readout converge on Q's. No jump, no teleporting — the point moves continuously with the angle.

demo_steps.title: Both sides, same destination
demo_steps.narration: Press play on the animation: x approaches c first from below, then from above. Each time P arrives at the same point Q — the two-sided limit exists and equals the function value.

demo_steps.title: Any c works
demo_steps.narration: Now drag c somewhere else on the circle and approach it again with x. The same shrinking-sector behavior occurs everywhere, which is why sine and cosine are continuous at every real number c.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because a point on the unit circle moves continuously as its angle changes, shrinking the angle gap x − c to zero forces the coordinates (cos x, sin x) onto (cos c, sin c) — the geometry of the circle is itself the proof that sine and cosine are continuous at every c.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Unit circle centered at the origin with arrow-tipped axes; the circle is solid blue through the region containing P and Q and becomes dashed on the far upper-left and lower-left arcs (a textbook styling cue to keep). P (red) sits at the smaller angle, Q (blue) at the larger; the radius to P is red, the radius to Q is black. Small angle arcs at the origin labeled italic serif 'x' and 'c'. The sector between the two radii is filled with a purple radial gradient, most intense near Q and fading toward the origin. Point labels are italic serif math text: 'Q(cos c, sin c)' above-right of Q and 'P(cos x, sin x)' right of P, each with the dot color matching its point. A short curved arrow near Q points along the circle in the direction P travels. Place a compact live readout (x, c, and both coordinate pairs, color-matched red/blue) in a corner so dragging visibly connects angle change to coordinate change. The caption box sits below the figure with a light gray border and centered text. Default view shows c ≈ 1.1 rad and x ≈ 0.5 rad, both in the first quadrant, matching the textbook composition.

authoredContext:
Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of sin x and cos x are drawn as continuous curves. We will not formally prove that these functions are continuous, but we can motivate this fact by letting c be a fixed angle in radian measure and x a variable angle in radian measure. If, as illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, the angle x approaches the angle c, then the point P(cos x,sin x) moves along the unit circle toward Q(cos c,sin c), and the coordinates of P approach the
corresponding coordinates of Q. This implies that
lim
x→c
sin x = sin c and limx→c
cos x = cos c (1)
Thus, sin x and cos x are continuous at the arbitrary point c; that is, these functions are continuous everywhere.

discrepancies: the bottom caption box shows only 'As x approaches c the point' — the second line 'P approaches the point Q.' is missing/clipped in the rendered output (tspan line breaking is unreliable), and fragments of that text appear garbled at the top-left near the readout box
the source's single curved arrow sits outside the arc near Q pointing toward it; the generated arrow is present but tiny and high, partially colliding with the Q label area

the shaded sector in the source spans from the x-axis up to Q (angle c); the generated figure shades only the small wedge between x and c, which is a reasonable pedagogical choice but differs visually from the source composition
the readout panel and the UI control panel add chrome not in the source, slightly changing the at-a-glance look, though the core circle/axes/sector/radii composition is preserved
evaluation.notes: The circle, axes, dashed left arcs, radii, P/Q dots, and angle arcs match the source well, and the x/c sliders plus two-sided approach animation with demo steps are genuinely strong interactions; the main blemishes are the broken caption second line leaking as garbled text at the top-left and the readout text crowding its box.
action_items: Fix the caption rendering: tspan .move() positioning is unreliable — replace with two separate text lines positioned explicitly inside the box (or an SVG <foreignObject>/plain tspans with x/dy set via attr), so 'P approaches the point Q.' renders inside the box and never leaks to the top-left.
Enlarge the readout box or shrink its font so the three readout lines fit cleanly inside the rounded rect without crowding.
Move the curved arrow slightly away from the Q label and lengthen it to match the source's prominent arc arrow, avoiding the near-collision with 'Q(cos c, sin c)'.
